Posted July 16, 2001
(MarijuanaNews note: Yes, the best two word explanation of marijuana prohibition is still " bad journalism. " However, the problem does not necessarily start with the popular press.

The UK and most of the western world is engaged in a debate about marijuana prohibition.

However, some of the reports sound like echoes from the 1930’s – true reefer madness, linking cannabis use and violence. The first item is the end of a chain of distortion that began with an interesting study from New Zealand. The items below, are in reverse order of their publication.

As you will see, the policy implications of what the research actually said are exactly opposite of what the headlines imply.)

July 13, 2001
From The Irish Examiner
exam_letters@examiner.ie
http://www.examiner.ie/
By John von Radowitz
REPORT SENDS 'MELLOW' CANNABIS THEORY UP IN SMOKE

Young men who take cannabis are five times more likely to be violent than those who avoid the drug, it was claimed today.

The findings are at odds with the popular perception of cannabis as a drug that makes people mellow.

They emerge from the first study to investigate the overlap between mental disorders and violence.

Psychiatrists looked at 961 adults born in Dunedin, New Zealand, between April 1972 and March 1973.

They were monitored every three years until the age of 26.

At the age of 21, a total of 34% of the young men in the group with a cannabis habit had a court conviction for violence, or reported violent behaviour in the previous year.
(MarijuanaNews note: Notice that we have already gone from " Young men who take cannabis " to " the group with a cannabis habit. " )

This represented a five-fold higher violence risk than the general population. It was also higher than the three-fold risk increase associated with men suffering from schizophrenia or dependent on alcohol.

The findings were presented today at the Royal College of Psychiatrists' annual meeting in London.

They showed that 40% had mental disorders and were five times more likely to be violent than those without mental conditions.

Dr Louise Arseneault, from the Institute of Psychiatry in London, who led the study, said:

" There is a substantial minority of young adults with specific mental disorders who are responsible for a substantial proportion of violence in the community.

" Not all mentally-ill individuals engage in violence. The link is limited to three groups -- those dependent on alcohol, those dependent on cannabis, and adults with schizophrenia. "

She said people with at least one of the disorders constituted a fifth of the sample, but accounted for more than half the convictions for violence.

" People with two of these disorders have an increased risk for violence eight to 18 times greater than that for people with no disorders, " she added.

Copyright: Examiner Publications Ltd, 2001

2001: A Mind Odyssey: Science and Caring
9th to 13th July 2001
Queen Elizabeth II Conference Centre
London SW1

Press Release from Royal College of Psychiatrists

Cannabis is not as mellow a drug as its supporters believe. Far from chilling out, young men who habitually use the drug are five times more likely to be violent than men who spurn marijuana.
(MarijuanaNews note: First, notice that the category here is clearly identified as " young men who habitually use " or " abuse " cannabis – clearly not all users, but the first sentence of the release – " Cannabis is not as mellow a drug as its supporters believe. " —sets the tone for the Irish Examiner story, so the problem did not begin with the popular press.

However, as we will see in the excerpts below this, that what is missing is the important part: The violence has nothing to do with cannabis use, per se.)

The findings were presented at the annual meeting by Dr Louise Arseneault, a lecturer in developmental psychology at the Institute of Psychiatry in London and are the results from a major study in New Zealand, the first study looking at the overlap between mental disorders and violence in young men.

Previously scientists thought there was only a moderate risk for someone with a mental disorder to have an increased tendency to violence, but researchers have traditionally concentrated on the age group from 25 to 40, -men who have been discharged from mental hospital. However, the peak age for violence is 14 to 22 and most of those men will never have been admitted to hospital. " Psychiatrists were not reporting the age group responsible for the most violence, " said Dr Arseneault.
(MarijuanaNews note: This is also the age cohort that has the highest levels of cannabis use.

Young males generally have disproportionately high levels of most social problems, such as auto accidents, drunkenness, violence in general, etc., so – even after legalization -- there will continue to be some correlation between marijuana use and social problems, at least until the aging baby-boomers increase their use of medical marijuana – or come out of the closet about their recreational use.)

The New Zealand study looked at 961 young adults born in Dunedin, New Zealand, between April 1972 and March 1973, 94 per cent of the total number of babies born in the city. Researchers followed them up every three years until the age of 15 and then at 18, 21 and 26.

They found that 40 per cent of the sample had mental disorders and were five times more likely to be violent than those without mental conditions and that though the group were found to suffer from a variety of mental conditions, such as anxiety, depression, mania and eating disorders, the association with violence was strong in only three.
(MarijuanaNews note: Many cannabis users are self-medicating for these conditions.)

Dr Arseneault and her colleagues found that in men violent behaviour and court convictions for violence were " uniquely associated " with those who had schizophrenia or who were dependent on alcohol or marijuana. At 21 a 34 per cent of the adults dependent on cannabis had a court conviction for violence or reported violent behaviour in the previous year (a fivefold risk over the general population) compared with a figure of 25.5 per cent for men dependent on alcohol (a threefold increase) and 25.5 per cent of men with schizophrenia.

" There is a substantial minority of young adults with specific mental disorders who are responsible for a substantial proportion of violence in the community, " said Dr Arseneault.

" Not all mentally ill individuals engage in violence; the link is limited to three group - those dependent on alcohol, those dependent on cannabis and adults with schizophrenia. People with at least one of these three disorders constituted one fifth of the sample, but accounted for more than half the violent convictions. Having two of these disorders. People with two of these disorders had an increased risk for violence eight to 18 times greater than that for people with no disorders. "

(MarijuanaNews note: To make matters even worse, this is not even a new story. It was first reported much more responsibly last October, by Reuters, based on a study published in the October issue of the Archives of General Psychiatry. Of course, it will now be immortalized with the sensationalist and misleading headlines.)

October 12, 2000
From Reuters
VIOLENCE LINKED TO SCHIZOPHRENIA, DRUG DEPENDENCY
NEW YORK ( Reuters Health )

Alcohol dependency, marijuana dependency and schizophrenia are strongly related to violence, researchers report.

``Our study suggests that a significant proportion of the burden of violence that frightens and injures the general public may be attributed to young adults who are prone to schizophrenia...or dependent on alcohol or other drugs, many of whom have not been hospitalized or treated,'' according to Dr. Louise Arseneault of the University of London, UK, and colleagues.

In their study, 961 young adults ( age 21 ) who resided in Dunedin, New Zealand were assessed for mental disorders and violence using both self-reported information and court records. The findings are published in the October issue of the Archives of General Psychiatry.

``Persons with at least one of these three disorders constituted only one fifth of the ( number of people evaluated ), but they accounted for more than half of the...violent convictions, violent acts and violent offenders ( committed by the group as a whole ),'' Arseneault and colleagues write.

Obviously, not all people with mental disorders engage in violence, the authors note. Nonetheless, the three disorders discussed in the report had a very high association with violent acts.

The report indicates that schizophrenic patients are more likely to harbor feelings of mistrust towards society, which may lead to violent acts during ``episodes of psychosis''--periods of loss of contact with reality.

On the other hand, those who are alcohol-dependent may simply be experiencing the ``disinhibiting effects'' associated with alcohol abuse, according to the researchers.

Recognition of this fact may be crucial in trying to stem violence among alcohol users through minimizing their use of alcohol, the team notes.

Marijuana users, having exposed themselves to illegal acts as in the buying and selling of illicit drugs ``may learn early to rely on violence for addressing disputes,'' the researchers suggest.

``Scientists and professionals do not welcome this finding because it stigmatizes these individuals,'' the authors write. ''However, research that provides sound explanations for the link may help to reduce ignorance that fuels public fears and to inform strategies for preventing or limiting violence among the mentally ill,'' Arseneault and colleagues conclude.

Excerpt From the Archives of General Psychiatry 2000;57:979-986.

Individuals meeting diagnostic criteria for alcohol dependence, marijuana dependence,

Persons with at least 1 of these 3 disorders constituted one fifth of the sample, but they accounted for half of the sample's violent crimes (10% of violence risk was uniquely attributable to schizophrenia-spectrum disorder).

Among alcohol-dependent individuals, violence was best explained by substance use before the offense; among marijuana-dependent individuals, by a juvenile history of conduct disorder

Rather, there is a level of violence that comes from its illegal status.

" Among alcohol-dependent individuals, violence was best explained by substance use before the offense; among marijuana-dependent individuals, by a juvenile history of conduct disorder… "

This is consistent with other reports that behavioral problems generally precede marijuana use.

The effects of all drugs are influenced by " set and setting " – the mindset and social and physical setting in which the drug is used. This is particularly true of cannabis, the effects of which are relatively subtle, in comparison with other drugs, especially alcohol.

Cannabis prohibition creates the worst possible " set and setting " -- especially for young users with troubled backgrounds and underlying emotional and psychological problems.

Dealing marijuana in a context of prohibition, with marijuana sold in the same markets as hard drugs is even more likely to produce a correlation with violence.

In a very violent culture, such as in the Jamaican slums, there may be a correlation between ganja and violence, but there is also a mixing of the ganja markets and hard drugs. Indeed, the recent outbreak of violence in the Kingston slums is described as being a battle between gangs fighting over the cocaine business.

People who think that they are being " conservative " or " cautious " by favoring only the decriminalization of possession rather than full legalization of possession, cultivation and sale of cannabis are in fact contributing to the problems associated with cannabis. This conclusion is very strongly supported by the study so appalling distorted here by both the Irish Examiner and the press release from Royal College of Psychiatrists.

Once again, cannabis has been blamed for the consequences of cannabis prohibition.
